newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Blair tries to end bout of infighting.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Blair tries to end bout of infighting.

text.p: Opposition leader Tony Blair tried on Monday to stop a week of ideological in-fighting by urging his Labour Party to focus on challenges facing Britain instead of political "froth and hype".
But Blair risked fuelling a damaging internal row over the direction of the party by defending a spokesman who said it was time to drop the word "socialism" from Labour's vocabulary.

Blair said the kernel of the argument deployed by Kim Howells, a junior industry spokesman, was absolutely correct: if socialism was about state control and nationalisation, it was not for the revamped Labour party of the 1990s.

"I agree absolutely that what we have got to be about is the best practical means to deliver a different type of society in Britain today that faces that modern world, that is based absolutely on our values, but isn't tied to some outdated form of ideology," Blair told BBC radio.
But anxious to maintain discipline in the run-up to the election, which must be held by next May, Blair told his spokesmen to think twice before they spoke out in public.
"Of course people have got to be careful because there is a different media climate about," the Labour leader said.

As Blair was speaking, the Conservatives unveiled a new poster showing the average British family 700 pounds ($1,089) a year better off than at the 1992 general election and warning that tax-raising Labour was eager to grab the extra cash.
Conservative Party chairman Brian Mawhinney denied that the poster, which again uses the controversial image of "demon eyes" to depict Labour, was negative campaigning.
"Life is getting better. It is going to get better still. That is the positive message of success. We are reminding people that they should not put that at risk," he told reporters.

Blair's forced march to the centre ground of British politics since he took over the party two years ago has earned Labour a 20-point lead in opinion polls among voters apparently tired of 17 unbroken years of Conservative rule.
But his haste in abandoning the party's ideological baggage and symbols has caused deep misgivings among traditional left-wingers.
Their unease grew last week following reports that Labour might one day sever ties with Britain's trade unions, which founded the party 90 years ago.
Blair said he had no plan in his back pocket to end links to the unions but acknowledged that the process of change he had initiated had been difficult for some in the party to accept.
Yet now it was more ideologically united than he had ever known it and he dismissed talk of divisions as "froth and hype".
The key question, Blair said, was whether a rejuvenated Labour party was able to address four "millennium challenges" facing Britain.

These were: how to compete in the new global market; how to create a modern welfare state and a cohesive society; how to make politics more in touch with the people; and how to regain influence for Britain abroad.
"In the end those are the things I care about. I care about changing the Labour party to make the Labour party the vehicle for answering those questions in the correct way," he said.
